newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bankgesellschaft-NordLB linkup possible, but hard.
newsitem.headline: Bankgesellschaft-NordLB linkup possible, but hard.

text.p: Bankgesellschaft Berlin AG said on Wednesday it was sure a tie-up with Norddeutsche Landesbank was possible but that a whole range of difficult issues had to be resolved first and that the process would take several years.

In a move which fuelled speculation about mergers in Germany's overcrowded bank sector, the two banks last month got the go-ahead from their owners -- several federal states in northern and eastern Germany -- to intensify talks about increasing cooperation.

"A legal link-up of the two big banking groups requires that additional business advantages can evolve from it," Hubertus Moser, one of two chief executives on the management board, told the bank's nine-month news conference.
"We are sure that this can be the case if certain preconditions are met about which we are in talks with our colleagues at NordLB. But we are under no time pressure."
A merger would create one of Germany's biggest banking groups with assets of more than 500 billion marks ($328.4 billion).
Moser said the two banks should come up with concrete proposals within the next six months but that it would take years to complete a tie-up, which would need the approval of four federal states.

For example, questions such as where the investment banking activities of a merged group would be based were highly sensitive political issues, said Wolfgang Steinriede, Bankgesellschaft's co-chief executive.

Norddeutsche Landesbank is 40 percent owned by the state of Lower Saxony. The east German states of Saxony-Anhalt and Mecklenburg-Vorpommern own 10 percent each and the remaining shares are owned by savings banks in the three states.

Bankgesellschaft, 56.8 percent owned by the state of Berlin, was formed in 1994 through the fusion of three banking groups from the public and private sectors -- Berliner Bank AG, Landesbank Berlin and Berliner Hypotheken und Pfandbriefbank.

NordLB and Bankgesellschaft have been cooperating since 1994. They have set up a joint software development subsidiary, merged their mortgage banking operations and formed a consultancy to advise public sector bodies on project finance.
Moser said a link-up was bound to result in economies of scale. "But that is not enough. The question is, will we get the structure to secure sufficient potential to pay dividends."

Analysts have said a merger could set the ball rolling for several big German banks to follow suit to rationalise their inefficient branch networks and gain the critical mass needed to survive fierce competition after European monetary union.
With over 3,600 commercial, public and cooperative banks vying for market share, and a rate of one branch per 1,100 inhabitants, Germany is already regarded as heavily overbanked.
But analysts see limited scope for cost savings from a merger between Bankgesellschaft and NordLB and say the main motivation for a tie-up is to replenish depleted state coffers.

The state of Berlin, desperately short of cash with debts of 50 billion marks, wants to sell more shares in Bankgesellschaft but cannot cut its stake below 50 percent without losing its status as guarantor of the bank's debt.
Without a government backer, the bank's credit rating would fall and the cost of refinancing would consequently rise.

Analysts say pooling the four states' stakes in a merged Bankgesellschaft/NordLB would pave a way for a significant sale of shares to the private sector while keeping the public stake above 50 percent.

"The idea for a link-up comes from the owners, not the from banks themselves," said Dieter Hein, banking analyst at BHF-Bank AG in Frankfurt. "The states want to plug their financial holes by selling off the silver." ($ = 1.522 German Marks)
